translations.text: Of the kinds of monks. It is known that there are four kinds of monks. The first is that of the cenobites, that is, the monastic kind, fighting under a rule or an abbot (father).
Then the second kind is that of the anchorites, that is, the hermits (forest-dwellers): those who, not in the fresh fervour of a new life,

but through long probation in the monastery, have learned to fight against the devil, already taught by the help of many; and, well taught, they go from the testing among the brothers to the solitary fight of the wilderness. Secure now, without another's help, they are able, with God helping, to fight with their own hand or arm against the vices of the flesh and of the thoughts.

The third kind of monks, and certainly the worst, is that of the sarabaites. They have not been tested by a rule and by the experience of a master, as gold is tested in the furnace, but are softened like the nature of lead. Still serving the world by their works, they are known to lie in their faith to God by their tonsure. They live in twos or threes, or even alone, without a shepherd, enclosed not in the Lord's sheepfolds but in their own. For their law is the pleasure of their desires. Whatever they think or choose,
that they call holy, and what they do not want, that they consider not permitted.

The fourth kind of monks is called that of the wanderers (gyrovagues). All their life long they go through various provinces and are lodged as guests in various cells for three or four days at a time. They are always wandering and never stable, serving their own wills and the unlawful enticements of the gullet, and in all things worse than the sarabaites.

Of the wretched way of life of all these it is better to be silent than to speak. Leaving these aside, then, let us come, with the Lord's help, to set in order the strongest kind, that of the cenobites.
He who is worthy to be over a monastery must always remember what he is called, and fulfil the name of the greater (superior) by his deeds.
For he is believed to act in the place of Christ in the monastery, since he is called by Christ's own name, as the apostle says:

"You have received the spirit of adoption of sons, in which we cry: Abba, Father." And therefore he must not teach, establish, or command anything outside the Lord's precept, far be it from him. Rather, let his command and his teaching be sprinkled into the minds of the disciples like the leaven of divine justice. Let him always be mindful that in the fearful judgment of God there will be an examination of his teaching and of the obedience of his disciples, of both matters.
And let him know that whatever less profit the father of the household can find in the sheep is laid to the fault of the shepherd.
But it is likewise so that, if all diligence has been applied by the shepherd to a restless or disobedient flock, and every care has been applied to their sick deeds,
their shepherd, acquitted in the Lord's judgment, may say to the Lord with the prophet: "I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have spoken your truth and your salvation.
But they, despising me, scorned me." And then at last, for the sheep disobedient to his care, let death itself be the punishment that prevails over them.
"He who hears you hears me." Truly, such as these at once leave what is theirs, abandoning their own will, at once with occupied hands

leave unfinished what they were doing, and with the near foot of obedience they follow the voice of the one commanding with deeds. And so, as if in a single moment, the master's command once spoken and the disciple's finished work are both carried out together quickly, in the swiftness of the fear of God,
by those who are pressed by the love of going to eternal life. Therefore they seize the narrow way, of which the Lord says:

"Narrow is the way that leads to life." So, not living by their own judgment, nor obeying their desires and wills, but walking by another's judgment and command, living in community, they desire [?] to be over them.

Without doubt such as these imitate the Lord's saying, in which he says: "I came not to do my own will, but the will of the Father who sent me." But this same obedience is acceptable to God and sweet to men only

if what is commanded is done not hesitantly, not lukewarmly, not slowly, nor with murmuring or with the answer of one who is unwilling, because obedience given to superiors is given to God. For he himself said: "He who hears you hears me."

And it ought to be given by disciples with a good heart, for [?] loves a cheerful giver. For if the disciple obeys with an ill heart, and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, then even if he fulfils the command, it is no longer acceptable to God,
who sees his heart murmuring. For such a deed no grace follows; rather he incurs the punishment of murmurers, unless he makes amends with due satisfaction.
Let us do what the prophet said: "I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue.
I set a guard on my mouth. I was struck dumb and humbled, and I kept silent even from good things."

Here the prophet shows that if we should sometimes keep silent even from good speech for the sake of silence, how much more should we refrain from evil words because of the punishment of sin. Therefore, even though perfect disciples are allowed to speak about good, holy and edifying things, permission to speak is granted only rarely, because of the seriousness of silence. For it is written: "In much speaking you will not escape sin." And in another place it says: "Death and life are in the power of the tongue."
Truly, it is fitting for the master to speak and teach; it is proper for the disciple to keep silent and listen.
Therefore, if anything has to be asked of superiors, let it be asked with the utmost reverence, so that one does not seem to speak more than is needful.
But jests, idle words, and words that stir up laughter we condemn everywhere and shut out forever. And we do not allow a disciple to open his mouth for such talk.

Holy Scripture cries out to us, saying: "Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted." When it says this, it shows us that every exaltation is a kind of pride. The prophet shows that he guards himself against this when he says:
"Lord, my heart is not exalted, nor are my eyes lifted up, nor have I walked in great things, nor in wonders beyond me.

Hence Scripture commands, saying: "Do not go after your desires." Truly, if the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the evil, and he always looks down from heaven upon the children of men, to see whether there is anyone who understands or seeks God,
and if our works are reported daily, by day and by night, to the Lord our maker by the angels assigned to us, then one must truly be on guard at every hour,

as the prophet says in the psalm, lest God see us at any hour turning aside into evil and become useless. And though he spares us in this time, because he is merciful and waits for us daily to be turned toward the better, let him not say to us in the time to come: "These things you did, and I kept silent."
The second step of humility is if someone, not loving his own will, takes no delight in fulfilling his desires, but imitates in deeds that voice
of the one [?] saying: "I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me." Again Scripture says: "Self-will has punishment, and necessity brings forth a crown."
The third step of humility is that someone, for the love of God, submits himself in all obedience to a superior, imitating the Lord, of whom the Apostle says: "He became obedient even unto death."

The fourth, if in this same obedience, when things are hard and contrary, or even when any injuries whatever are inflicted, he embraces [?] with a silent mind, and enduring does not grow weary or go away, as Scripture says: "He who perseveres

to the end, he shall be saved." Likewise: "Let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord." And showing that the faithful man must endure all things for the Lord, even contrary things, it says in the person of those who suffer: "For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are reckoned as sheep for the slaughter." [?]
And secure in the hope of the divine reward, they follow after, rejoicing and saying: "But in all these things we overcome through him who loved us."
Likewise in another place: "You have tested us; you have tried us with fire, as silver is tried with fire.
You led us into the snare; you laid hardship upon our back."
And to show that we must be under a superior, it follows, saying: "You set men over our heads." And also the command

[?] in adversities and injuries: those who are struck on the cheek offer the other as well; to the one who takes away the tunic they also give up the cloak; when forced to go one mile, they go two; and with Paul the Apostle they endure false brothers, and endure persecution, and bless those who speak evil of them.
The fifth, if he does not conceal, through humble confession, all the evil thoughts that come into his heart, or the evils he has done in secret,
from his own [?], Scripture urging us concerning this matter and saying: "Reveal your way to the Lord and hope in him."
Again: "Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever." Again: "I made my transgression known to you; [?] I covered my injustices.
I said: I will declare my injustice against myself, Lord, and you forgave the impiety of my sin." The sixth, if a monk, content with every meanness and utmost lowliness,

in all the things that are laid on him, he judges himself a bad and unworthy workman, saying to himself with the prophet: "I have been brought to nothing and I did not know it; I have become like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you."

The seventh, if he declares himself lower and baser than all, not only with his tongue but also believes it with the innermost love of his heart, humbling himself and saying with the prophet: "But I am a worm and not a man, a reproach of men and an outcast of the people"; "exalted, humbled, confounded"; and again: "It is good for me
that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your commandments!"

The eighth, if he does nothing except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders urge. If he keeps his tongue from speaking and, keeping silence, does not speak until he is asked, as Scripture says, that "in much speaking sin is not escaped" and that "a talkative man is not set straight upon the earth."
The tenth, if he is not easy and quick to laughter, for it is written: "The fool raises his voice in laughter." He speaks gently,
without laughter, humbly, with seriousness; he speaks few and reasonable words, and is not loud of voice, as it is written:
"The wise man is known by few words." The twelfth, if he always shows humility not only in his heart but also in his very body to those who see him, that is, in work,
in the garden,

on the road, in the field, or wherever he is, sitting, walking or standing, with his head always bowed and his eyes fixed on the ground; at every hour he considers himself guilty of his sins and thinks himself already brought before the dreadful judgment, always saying in his heart what the publican of the Gospel said with his eyes fixed on the ground: "I, a sinner, am not worthy to lift my eyes to heaven"; and again with the prophet: "I am bowed down and humbled on every side."
"So when all these steps of humility have been climbed, he will soon arrive at that love of God

which, being perfect, casts out fear. Through it he will begin to keep without any effort, as if naturally and from habit, everything he used to observe not without fear. He will keep it no longer out of fear of hell but out of love, and out of that same good habit, [and] the delight of the virtues. The Lord will deign to show this by the Holy Spirit in his workman, now cleansed of vices and sins.

In wintertime, according to the consideration of reason, one is to rise at the eighth hour of the night, so that one rests a little beyond midnight and rises likewise having digested. What remains after the vigils is to be used by those brothers who need some part of the psalter
or of the readings, for study. From
however,

to the time mentioned above, let the time be arranged so that the vigils are done with a very short interval, in which the brothers go out for the needs of nature. Immediately afterwards the morning lauds, which are to be done as the light begins, follow.

let him be chosen from the congregation: wise, of mature character, sober, not a great eater, not proud, not turbulent, not hostile-minded, not slow, not wasteful, but fearing God, one who shall be like a father to the whole congregation.
Let him take care of everything; let him do nothing without the abbot's command; let him keep to what is commanded; let him not sadden [the brothers].

If anyone asks him for something unreasonable at some time, let him not sadden him by spurning him, but reasonably and with humility refuse the one who asks wrongly. Let him guard his own soul, always mindful of that apostolic saying, that "he who ministers well acquires a good standing for himself."
Let him take care of the sick, of children, of guests and of the poor with all solicitude, knowing without doubt that he will have to render account for all these on the day of judgement.
Let him regard all the vessels and all the property as though they were the consecrated vessels of the altar.

Let him treat nothing as something to neglect, and let him not be wasteful or an uprooter of the property of the monastery, but let him do everything in measure and according to the command of the abbot.
...if it is a day of fasting, then when Vespers have been said, after a short interval let them soon come together, as we have said, and when four [or] five leaves have been read
or as much as the time permits, while all run together into one place during this delay of the reading

[and if anyone] is occupied in the [task] assigned and entrusted to him, [let him come]. Let all, gathered together, complete [Compline], and when they go out from it, let there be no leave for anyone to speak again. But if anyone is found to transgress this rule of silence, let him be subject to the heavier punishment, unless the needs of guests come upon them, or [someone gives] someone something [?]; yet let this too be done with the greatest gravity and moderation, most honourably.

At the time of the divine office, as soon as the signal has been heard, let them leave everything that is in their hands and run with the greatest haste, yet with gravity, so that foolery does not find tinder. Certainly let nothing be put before the Work of God. At the night vigils, [after the psalm] which we wish to be said slowly and drawn out for that reason, [if anyone] does not come in [in time],

[let him not stand] in his order, but let him stand last of all, or in a place set apart for such careless ones, so that they may be seen by him and by all, until, [when the Work of God] has been completed, they do penance by public satisfaction. [We have judged that they] ought to stand in the last place, so that, being seen by all, they may amend because of that very shame.

For if they remain outside the church, [there may be someone who] lies down and sleeps, or certainly sits outside by himself and is free [?] for idle tales, and an opening is given to the accursed one. [Rather] let them go in, so that they do not lose everything and may make amends from then on.
At the daytime
hours, [whoever] for the Work of God
does not come in [in time], by the law which we stated above

to join [the choir] [?] until the act of satisfaction, [unless] by leave of his remission [?]; [that all] may come up together as one. But if anyone, [through negligence] or vice, [does not come in time]

up to the second time, let him be rebuked for this; if he still does not amend, let him not be allowed to share [the common table], but, separated from the fellowship [of all], [let him eat] alone, with his portion taken from him, until amendment [?]; likewise
let him suffer, [who is not] present [?]
[at the verse] said after the meal
[before the] appointed [hour]
or after it, [let no one presume to take] anything of food
or drink. But also, if something is brought to someone and he refuses it, at the time when he desires what he refused before, or something else, [let him receive nothing] until fitting amendment.

[Those who] are excommunicated for grave sins, [at the hour when the Work of God] is celebrated, let him lie stretched out in front of the doors of the church, saying nothing, except only, having placed
his head [on the ground], prostrate face down at the feet of those going out, let him fold [himself] before them [?]
until satisfaction has been made; then, [when] he has been commanded,
let him throw himself down before the footprints of the same [abbot] and then [of all], in the order [the abbot decides], so that he does not presume to raise [a psalm or reading] or anything else
when [the Work of God] is completed, let him throw himself down
in the place where he stands; and let him make satisfaction in this way [until he is told] to rest from the act of satisfaction. For lighter [faults], to perform [it] thus at the command is enough.
If anyone makes a mistake while he is reciting [a psalm, responsory, antiphon or reading], [and] unless by an act of satisfaction

he is humbled before [all] [?] ..., let him be subject to the greater punishment, [as one who would not] correct by humility what he did wrong through negligence; but let children be beaten for such [a fault].
let him withdraw from his body some food, some drink, some sleep, some talk, some jesting, and with the joy of spiritual desire let him await holy Easter. This same

that which each one offers, let him make known to [?] (cote), and let it be done with his prayer and will, because what is done without [the permission] of the spiritual father is counted as presumption and vain glory, not reward. Therefore all things are to be done with [his] will.

care for the reception of the poor and of pilgrims [let it be shown] most attentively, because in them more [is] received; the terror of the rich itself demands honor for itself. Of the guests separately
at uncertain [?] hours [arriving], [the brothers] are disturbed
for the year, that same office; so [when] they have need, let help be given to them

murmuring; [when] they have less occupation, let it be commanded by them [where they are to go]; in the offices let this consideration be [kept], [that help be] granted; [when] free [?], obeying those who command. Likewise the chamber

it is commanded, in no way let him associate with or speak with [them]; [if he] meets [them], greeting humbly, as we said, the blessing having been asked, let him pass on, [saying] it is not permitted to him to speak with a guest.
In no way is it permitted, neither from kinsmen nor from anyone, nor among themselves, [to receive or give] letters or any gifts whatsoever
anything that has been sent, [unless] it has been made known, to be received; in the power [of the abbot], to whom it is commanded to be given; to whom [?] (frist) of the regular discipline
clothing, according to the qualities of places, of the temperature of the air; in cold regions more is needed, in warm ones less. This
consideration. We [believe it] sufficient in moderate places for each one a cowl, in winter shaggy, in summer thin or old; coverings of the feet, [?] (suueif)
shoes; about the color or coarseness of these things let them not complain; region; what can be bought more cheaply; let him provide for the measure
short, those same clothes, for those wearing them, [but] measured; receiving new ones, let them give back the old ones at once, to be put away in the wardrobe; it suffices

to wash those same things; what is over [and above] is superfluous, [it must be] cut off; so what was old [let them return]. Breeches: those who are sent [on a journey], let them receive [them] from the wardrobe; those returning, [let them restore them] washed; somewhat better than the usual ones which they have, a little better, which those going out [on a journey receive]. Bedding, sufficient
a mat, a blanket, a coverlet, a pillow; [the beds] are to be searched because of private property; to whom there is found [anything], [let him be subject to the discipline] most severe

let him be subject. So that the vice of private ownership may be cut off by the roots, which are necessary: shoes, belt, towel; that every excuse be taken away; by whom let be considered that saying [of the Acts], that it was given to each one as to each was needful; of the needy, the evil
of the envious
of judgments, retribution
of pilgrims; as often as fewer guests [are present], [whom he wishes] of the brothers to call [is] in his own power; elders to be left [with the brothers]
craftsmen, with all humility
those same arts; [if the abbot] permits; if any of them is puffed up on account of the knowledge of his art, because it seems that he contributes something
such a one, let him be removed from that same art; again, [unless] humbled. If something of the works of the craftsmen is to be sold
[?] of whatever [kind] [?] to go, in any trial let them be mindful [?], suffered in the body, than these [?]
any necessity be endured. In the same
let [the evil of] greed not creep in, but let it be priced somewhat more cheaply than by worldly people.
Let entry not be made easy for one newly coming to the [monastic] life; test the spirits; [if] he perseveres knocking, [and] the injuries inflicted [on him] and the difficulty
is seen to bear patiently, [and] to persist in his petition, let entry be granted him, [and let him be] in the guests' quarters a few [days], [then in the quarters] of the novices, where they study

let such a senior be assigned [to them] as is fit to win [souls], [who will] carefully watch over [them]; [and let there be] concern whether [he truly seeks God], [is] eager for the work [of God], for obedience

reproaches; [let] the hard and harsh things [be told to him] by which one goes [to God]. [If he promises] his stability, persevering, after the circuit of two [months] let this rule be read [to him] in order

["Behold] the law under which you wish to fight; [if] you can keep [it, enter; if not], depart free." Then [if] he still [stands firm, let him be led into] the aforementioned [quarters] and be tested [in all patience]; [after a] circuit [of months] let the commands be read [to him] again

knowing that it is established by law that it is not permitted [to him] to go out [of the monastery] [or] to shake off [his neck] from under the yoke [of the rule], under such deliberate [consideration] it was permitted [?] [him] from [being] free [?]
to refuse [?]

Let the one to be received promise concerning stability, life, morals [and] obedience [before God and His] saints, [that] if ever [he acts] otherwise, [he should know he will be] condemned [by Him whom]

he mocks. Concerning that profession [let him make] a petition in the name of the saints [whose] relics [are there] and of the [abbot] present; [let him write it with his own hand, or if he does not know] letters, [another] being asked [may write it], [and let] the novice [make his] sign
[and] lay [it on the altar]; which [verse] then each one [of the community answers] a third time
adding [the Gloria]. [Then] the novice is to prostrate himself at the feet [of each, that they may pray] for him; from that day let him be counted [in the community].

[As for his] possessions, if he has any, [let him give them to the poor or], a solemn donation having been made, confer [them on the monastery], keeping [nothing] for himself of all, since indeed [from that day he will not have power even] over his own body.

[Then in the oratory] let him be stripped of his own [things] with which he was clothed, [and] be clothed [in the monastery's things]; let the clothes of which he was stripped be laid in the wardrobe to be kept

[so that if] ever, [the devil] persuading [him], he consents [to leave the monastery], stripped of [the monastery's] things he is to be cast out. [But] the petition which [the abbot took] from above [the altar] is to be kept [in the monastery].

[If anyone] of the nobles offers his son [to God], [and] that same child is of younger age, [let] the parents [make] the same petition [mentioned] above, [and] wrap the [hand] of the child [with it] in the [altar] cloth, [with] the offering, in the presence [?] [and so offer him].

[In] the petition [let them] promise under a proper oath that never [by themselves], [never] through a substituted person, [nor] in any manner whatever, [will they] ever give [him] anything [or] an occasion to have [it]

or [if they wish] to bring something [as alms] for [their] reward, [let them make a donation] of the things which [they wish to] give, the usufruct being reserved [to themselves], [if they so wish], [?] be kept.

[And let all be so blocked that] no suspicion remains to the child [by which], deceived, [he might] perish, [which] we have learned by experience. Likewise [let] the poorer [do]; simply, [before] witnesses.
[If anyone] of the order of priests [asks] to be received [in the monastery]

[let him not] be assented to too quickly. [If he] persists [in this request], [let him know he is] to keep all the discipline of the rule; [nothing] shall be relaxed [for him], [as it is written]: "Friend, for what [have you come]?" Let it be granted [him] to stand [after the abbot] [and] to bless
[and] to have [?]; otherwise [let him] by no means presume anything, knowing himself
subject [to the discipline of the rule].
